questions.question: Explain what oral history is and why it is important for studying apartheid.
questions.expected_answer: Oral history: collecting and studying memories through recorded interviews; first-hand accounts are primary sources (contrast secondary sources). Long African oral traditions (praise poems, izibongo, griots). Important because official records reflect the apartheid government's view, censorship, many voices (black, coloured, Indian, women, rural, poor) unrecorded; shows how laws affected families, and resistance; examples: TRC testimony, District Six Museum.

questions.question: Describe how to research an apartheid law and plan an ethical interview.
questions.expected_answer: Choose a law affecting your community: Population Registration Act 1950, Group Areas Act 1950, pass laws/Abolition of Passes Act 1952, Bantu Education Act 1953, Separate Amenities Act 1953, Mixed Marriages Act 1949, Immorality Amendment Act 1950. Research: when passed, contents, aims, enforcement, effects, resistance, repeal; textbooks, libraries, SAHO, archives; record references. Interview: suitable affected person; informed (written) consent, recording permission, anonymity, right to refuse or stop; prepared questions from background to law to reflection; open, non-leading questions; quiet place, record and take notes, listen, follow up, sensitivity; thank; transcribe promptly.

questions.question: Explain how to evaluate oral evidence and structure the research report.
questions.expected_answer: Memory can fade, mix events, reflect later knowledge and point of view; check first-hand vs second-hand, time elapsed and age, perspective, internal consistency, corroboration with written sources and others; differences may show local enforcement; usefulness vs reliability. Report: introduction with key question, background on the law, interview summary/extracts, analysis comparing sources, conclusion, bibliography including interview; own words, quotation marks and referencing, avoid plagiarism.
